cells.tense: You're at the bench today, and the work in your hands is the work you meant to be doing.
cells.ask: Before you close up, take one pass at something you'd normally leave as good enough, and stop when the pass is done — let that be the whole of it.
cells.core:
There's a table in your life your hands keep returning to, and the returning does its own clearing: what doesn't belong gets set aside and the real work gets room. You know which is which without having to decide it twice. Releasing and keeping happen in the same motion, and the keeping is where the skill grows. That steadiness is what people feel when they stand near your work, even when nothing is being said. Putting a thing down when it's finished is part of the same craft, not a gap in it.

The invitation here is small: let one more pass be enough for today. Rest is part of the work — it isn't a debt you're running up against tomorrow, and the bench will still be there.
cells.sheetLine: You know what to let go of by returning to what to keep.
cells.verb: standing at the bench where one piece is worked deeper than the last
cells.place: in the part of a life where release makes room by letting a gripped thing go

cells.tense: You're already at next year's bench, bracing, before this year's piece has had a chance to be finished.
cells.ask: Before you start, say one sentence out loud about what you're making and who it's for — and let the answer be small enough to finish today.
cells.core:
There's a table in your life where the work is honest and unfinished, and that unfinishedness is the point of it. In its steady form, the piece gets worked because it's in front of you — the next pass follows the last one without a forecast attached, and the doing is what the day is for.

Right now every pass is turning into a claim about how it will last, whether it was worth it, how it will be received, and that pressure is taking the bench away from you. Naming what you're making in the present, instead of the future, is the way back. Say it, and who it's for, in one sentence small enough to finish.

cells.tense: You're still standing in front of a door that's already behind you, and your hands haven't picked up the work in front of you.
cells.ask: Name one project you set down before finishing, and take the smallest possible next step on it today — one line, one pass, one phone call, whatever the smallest real thing is.
cells.core:
There's a table in your life with a half-finished thing on it. In its steady form, the next step is obvious because the hands are already there, and the finish is what makes room — what gets set down stays down because something else has taken its place.

The work is still in the room, and the practice has gone quiet. This isn't inability. It's a grip that has nothing left to hold, still holding, and the waiting is keeping the bench empty. A declared finish is the way back: take the smallest real step today, small enough that you can't argue with it, and let the step itself be the statement.

cells.tense: You're at the bench now, and it's the same bench you've been at — even if the hours have started feeling like someone else's.
cells.ask: At the end of the next working session, write one line on what actually moved — not what you meant to move, what moved — and keep it where the next session can find it.
cells.core:
There's a table in your life where things get made, and in its steady form the making is quiet and the maker is present in it — the work and the one doing it aren't strangers, and what gets kept and what gets released are chosen, not drifted into.

The hands keep choosing, and it can feel like the bench fills on its own, one piece after another, with no one in particular responsible. Moving from what the work did, not from what it was supposed to do, is the way back. Write one line after the next session about what actually moved, and keep it small enough to be true.

attempts.check: The draft risks claiming a long history of dedicated work and a felt threshold of mastery in the Balanced cell, which the record does not establish, so the core says the practice is daily and the threshold stays a condition, not an achievement. A reader could object that many people at a bench are just tired, not consecrated, so the ask stays a visible experiment that works even if the read is wrong. The sentence 'nobody handed this to you' serves the writer more than the reader, so I cut it; the Too Little ask is fine to re-run a process the person knows, since Assertion on glass is the act, not the outcome.
